extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, policymakers, and civil liberties advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles governing when society or government may legitimately interfere with individual liberty, with emphasis on freedom of thought, speech, association, and self-regarding conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Principle / Self-protection sole end
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection. The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant. Remonstration, persuasion, or exhortation may be used to promote an individual's good, but compulsion (legal penalties or other enforced sanctions) is justified only when the conduct is calculated to produce evil to some one else. This principle is meant to govern all compulsion by society, whether by law or by moral coercion of public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual sovereignty over body and mind (self-regarding liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the part which merely concerns himself, his independence is, of right, absolute. Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This domain covers inward consciousness, liberty of conscience, thought, feeling, opinions, tastes, pursuits, and the framing of one's life to suit one's own character. Such conduct should not be interfered with so long as it does not harm others, even if others consider it foolish or wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of thought, discussion, speaking and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete liberty of contradicting and disproving opinions is necessary: the liberty of thought and discussion (including expression and publication) is essential because silencing opinion robs mankind; if the opinion is right, others are deprived of truth, and if wrong, the collision with error clarifies truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silencing an opinion assumes infallibility. Free discussion is required to correct errors and to give the best attainable assurance of truth. The press and public debate must generally be free; the government has no rightful authority to prescribe opinions to the people or to silence dissent merely because it thinks them false or dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of tastes, pursuits, and lifestyle
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow: without impediment from our fellow-creatures, so long as what we do does not harm them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers actions that primarily affect only the actor; others may think the conduct perverse or foolish, but that does not justify coercion. The principle extends to personal conduct that affects others only with their free, voluntary, and undeceived consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of combination / association
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite, for any purpose not involving harm to others: the persons combining being supposed to be of full age, and not forced or deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consenting adults may form associations for purposes that do not harm others. This freedom is part of the sphere of individual liberty and only becomes subject to societal control when the association causes harm to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible compulsion to enforce duties benefiting others
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many positive acts for the benefit of others, which he may rightfully be compelled to perform; such as, to give evidence in a court of justice; to bear his fair share in the common defence, or in any other joint work necessary to the interest of the society of which he enjoys the protection; and to perform certain acts of individual beneficence, such as saving a fellow-creature's life, or interposing to protect the defenceless against ill-usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may cause evil to others by action or inaction; both can make him answerable to society. Holding someone responsible for omission (not preventing evil) requires more caution and is the exception rather than the rule, justified only in clear and grave cases. When enforcement is inadvisable, appeal should be to the agent's conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for those not of full maturity or societies 'in nonage'
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of individual liberty applies only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. We are not speaking of children, or of young persons below the age which the law may fix as that of manhood or womanhood. For backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage, despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsion and paternalistic measures may be legitimately used for those who require care or for societies not yet capable of being improved by free and equal discussion; once capable of guidance by persuasion, compulsion is no longer admissible except for protecting others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against tyranny of public opinion (social tyranny)
rubrics_metrics.description: There needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling; against the tendency of society to impose, by other means than civil penalties, its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social coercion—moral pressure, ostracism, or enforced conformity by opinion—can penetrate more deeply into life than political oppression and leave fewer means of escape; therefore limits must be found and maintained on the legitimate interference of collective opinion with individual independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward majority moral judgments and awareness of social bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Men's opinions on what is laudable or blamable are affected by multifarious causes: reason, prejudices, superstitions, social affections, envy, jealousy, arrogance, self-interest; where there is an ascendant class, much of the morality of the country emanates from its class interests and feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that prevailing moral standards frequently reflect class interests, servility to rulers or gods, or other partial motives. Those who assess or impose moral rules should be wary of mistaking custom or majority feeling for self-justifying truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of open challenge and discussion to justify coercive action
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete liberty of contradicting and disproving our opinion is the very condition which justifies us in assuming its truth for purposes of action; the steady habit of correcting and completing opinion by collating it with those of others is the only stable foundation for a just reliance on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (public or private) who claim to act on convictions should submit those convictions to public criticism and allow opportunities for refutation; to forbid propagation of an opinion on the ground of its supposed falsity is to preclude the only means of attaining rational assurance. Examples: the 'devil's advocate' in canonisation, the value of keeping lists open to attempts at refutation.
